## What is the course about?

- **Goal**: By the end of the day you can...
  - explain what version control changes for a research group
  - use branches and merge requests in GitLab to make and review a change (incl. one made with Claude Code)
  - take home a first draft of a shared Git guide for your group
- **Format**: Mix of input, practicals & discussion
  - Feel free to always ask questions any time!

# Why Version Control Matters for Research {background-color="black" background-opacity="0.3" background-image="images/backgrounds/yancy-min-842ofHC6MaI-unsplash.jpg"}

::: attribution
Background: https://unsplash.com/photos/842ofHC6MaI
:::

## Sounds Familiar? 📁

```text
analysis.py
analysis_v2.py
analysis_v2_final.py
analysis_v2_final_FINAL.py
analysis_v2_final_FINAL_comments-jan.py
```

::: {.fragment}
Version control replaces this with a single file and a full history of all its changes.
:::

## What is Version Control?

- Records all changes to your files over time
  - Who changed what, when and (ideally) why
- Allows you to go back to any previous version
- Allows multiple people to work on the same files at the same time
- The most common tool for this is `git` (more on that in Part 2)

## Why does it Matter for Research? 🔬

- Research increasingly depends on code
  - Analysis scripts, models, simulations, data processing, ...
- Results are only as trustworthy as the code that produced them
- Research code is often written by small and changing teams
  - Frequently without any formal training in software development

# Code as a Research Record

## Code as a Research Record 📜

- Like a lab notebook, a repository documents how results came about
- Each commit records what changed, when, by whom and why
- You can go back to exactly the version that was used for a paper, figure or dataset
  - Even years later

## Continuity: When People Move On 👋

- PhD students and postdocs leave, their code stays
- Without version control, code often lives on someone's laptop (or in someone's head)
- With a shared repository
  - Code is in a central place that the *group* owns
  - The history explains *why* things are the way they are
  - New people can pick up where others left off

## Discussion 💬

::: {.nonincremental}

- Where does the code of your group live right now?
- What would happen if the person who wrote it left tomorrow?

:::

# Review: Peer Review for Code

## Bringing Peer Review to Code 🔍

- We review papers before they are published, but code is rarely reviewed
- *Merge requests* bring a review step to code
  - Changes are proposed on a separate *branch*
  - Someone else looks at them, comments and approves them
  - Only then are they merged into the main version
- Catches errors early & spreads knowledge across the group

## Review Doesn't Have to be Heavy 🪶

- A second pair of eyes is already a big improvement
- Questions to ask in a review
  - Do I understand what this change does and why?
  - Does it do what it claims to do?
  - Could it break something else?
- We will practice this in Part 2

# AI Assistants and Accountability

## AI Coding Assistants 🤖

- Tools like Claude Code can read, write and change code in your projects
- They can save a lot of time
  - e.g. for documentation, refactoring or understanding unfamiliar code
- **But**: They also make mistakes, which can look very convincing

## Who is Accountable? ⚖️

- The person who merges a change is responsible for it
  - No matter who (or what) wrote it
- Version control makes changes by AI assistants visible & reviewable
  - Let the assistant work on a separate branch
  - Review its changes just like those of a colleague (via a merge request)

## Who is Accountable? Open Questions 🤔

Questions your group will need to answer:

- Which tools are we allowed to use?
- Which code and data may be shared with them?
- Should changes made with an AI assistant be marked as such?

# Open Science and Group Decisions

## Open Science 🔓

- Sharing code makes research more transparent and reproducible
- Journals and funders increasingly expect code to be available
- When making code public, also think about
  - A license, so others know how they are allowed to use it
    - To help you pick a license: <https://choosealicense.com/>
  - A `CITATION` file, so people know how to cite it
  - A DOI (digital object identifier), e.g. via [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/about)

## Decisions Your Group Needs to Make 🧭

Version control works best when a group agrees on how to use it.

- *Scope*: What goes into git (and what doesn't)?
- *Collaboration*: How do we change shared code?
- *AI assistants*: How do we work with tools like Claude Code?
- *Continuity*: How do we ensure reproducibility, publishing and handover?

::: {.fragment}
We will draft answers to these questions together in Part 3 ✍️
:::
